extracted.intended_audience: design owners, inventors, and IP practitioners considering international design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Explainer on using the Hague Agreement (WIPO) to obtain international design registration and how it compares to the PCT and national filing routes. Covers eligibility, filing mechanics, examination, scope, timing, and term considerations for design patents/registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliation requirement to use the Hague system
rubrics_metrics.description: To use the Hague system, you must be affiliated with (e.g., be a reside of) a contracting party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only applicants affiliated with a contracting party may file a Hague application; if not affiliated you must file directly in the desired country. Affiliation examples include residency. Filing through local IP offices is possible for applicants of that contracting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing route: direct with WIPO IB or via local IP office
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file for a Hague application directly with WIPO’s International Bureau (IB) or indirectly with a local intellectual property (IP) office of a contracting party, such as the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local IP offices forward Hague applications to the IB for processing. Filing through the USPTO automatically triggers review for foreign filing license; direct filing with IB may require a separate foreign filing license for U.S.-made inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of designs per Hague application
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague application may cover up to 100 designs belonging to the same International Classification of Industrial Designs (Locarno Classification), regardless of whether the designs are similar in appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some contracting parties impose a unity-of-design requirement (e.g., Japan and the U.S.) and may refuse the effects of an international registration if the unity requirement is not met. Be prepared for restriction/divisional practice in countries that require unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation timing and payment at filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague applicant designates contracting parties in which the Hague application is to be processed and pays corresponding fees at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with the PCT, where designation (national phase entry) and related filings/payments occur later (30/31 months). Designating and paying upfront affects strategy and costs at filing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: IB international-phase examination limited to formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague application is not substantively reviewed during the international phase. The IB conducts an initial review to make sure the Hague application conforms to formality requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formality requirements are met, the IB registers the design in the International Register. Substantive examination is performed later by local IP offices of designated contracting parties under their national laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication triggers local substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of your Hague application in the International Designs Bulletin automatically triggers examination by local IP offices of designated contracting parties under their local laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local offices may perform substantive examination or only a review similar to the IB. The outcome depends on each office’s procedures and standards; absence of refusal within a prescribed time generally causes the international registration to take effect in that party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and publication deferment
rubrics_metrics.description: The IB generally publishes the design in the International Designs Bulletin six months (except when publication deferment is possible and requested) after the international registration date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International registration date equals the later of the international filing date or the date irregularities are corrected. Requesting publication deferment can delay publication if allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of non-refusal by designated contracting party
rubrics_metrics.description: If an IP office of a contracting party does not issue a refusal to the IB within a prescribed time limit, then the international registration takes effect and provides protection as if the design had been registered or patented under local laws of the contracting party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of protection afforded depends on each party’s local law; some parties will automatically give effect, while others may issue refusals leading to local prosecution or amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in local substantive examination and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some local IP offices perform substantive examination, other local IP offices merely perform a similar review performed by the IB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in local examination practices and standards can mandate changes after filing or result in unintended effects on scope of protection where features of design representations are interpreted differently. Consider local requirements when preparing international drawings and disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and renewal of international registration
rubrics_metrics.description: An international registration is valid for at least 15 years of protection. The international registration is valid for the first five (5) years from the date of international registration and can be renewed up to the maximum duration of protection allowed in each of the designated contracting parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewal rules vary by contracting party; some parties provide for durations longer than the Hague baseline. Check national rules for renewal timing and fees. International registration minimums and local maximums should be planned for in portfolio management.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. term and fee treatment for Hague-derived design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S., the term for design patents resulting from applications filed on or after May 13, 2015, is 15 years from issuance. Payment of the fees for renewing the international registration ('renewal fees') is not required to maintain a U.S. patent issuing on an international design application in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although international registration renewals may be required for continued effect in some contracting parties, a U.S. design patent obtained from a Hague application does not require Hague renewal fees to maintain the U.S. patent in force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority deadline for Hague applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague application must be filed within six months of an earlier filed application in order to claim priority to that earlier filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from the PCT priority period (one year). Be mindful of the shorter six-month priority window when planning foreign filings and priority claims for designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication gives provisional rights in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Hague applications designated to the U.S. are published and can provide provisional rights to obtain damages for infringement that occurred between the publication date of the design and the issue date of the U.S. patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a U.S.-designated Hague application is published, any related U.S. design application that claims priority will also be made available for public access. Consider strategic implications of early publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of uniform drawing standards among contracting parties
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no uniform drawing standards among the contracting parties, and some contracting parties have fundamentally different requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in drawing/representation requirements can mandate post-filing changes or cause unexpected interpretations of scope. Prepare drawings with an eye to key designated jurisdictions and consider potential need for amendments or additional filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-contracting countries require direct national filing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you wish to seek protection in a country that is not a contracting party of the Hague Agreement (e.g., Taiwan; also note China and India are not contracting parties), you need to file directly in that country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hague system does not cover countries outside the contracting parties; budgeting and strategy must include direct national filings for those markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO restriction requirement and divisional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though the Hague application may include up to 100 designs, the USPTO will issue a restriction requirement if the application discloses more than one patentably distinct design, whereafter divisional applications can be filed for non-elected designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect restriction practice in the U.S.; plan for potential divisional filings and additional fees if multiple distinct designs are included in a single international application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing license considerations for U.S. inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. applicants should remember that a foreign filing license is required for an invention made in the U.S. to properly file the Hague application directly with the IB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a Hague application through the USPTO is automatically reviewed for a foreign filing license. If no request for a foreign filing license is included in a PCT application filed through the USPTO and it is clear that a foreign filing license is required, the USPTO will construe the filing to include such a request.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO national security refusal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO may refuse to forward a Hague application to the IB if doing so threatens national security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing through the USPTO carries an additional check for national security concerns which can prevent forwarding; consider this in filings involving sensitive technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: International registration date determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The international registration date is the later of the international filing date or the date of when irregularities in the Hague application are corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and certain time periods are measured from the international registration date; promptly addressing formal irregularities can affect publication timing and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope and growth of Hague contracting parties
rubrics_metrics.description: There are currently 74 contracting parties (covering 91 countries) to the Hague Agreement, including the U.S., Canada, Japan, and the EU (excluding the U.K.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number of contracting parties is growing, which expands the utility of the system over time. Assess current coverage for markets of interest before relying solely on Hague filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key differences between Hague system and PCT for strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: While both systems provide a streamlined filing process, PCT and Hague differ in important ways: PCT requires a single inventive concept; Hague allows up to 100 designs (subject to unity requirements), designation/payment timing differs, international-phase substantive search/exam differs, and priority periods differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these differences to choose an optimal filing route: PCT offers international search/report for utility patents to inform national phase decisions, while Hague centralizes designation at filing and relies on national substantive examination for designs. Consider timing, cost, and strategic flexibility.
